payload: Elon Musk's midnight-cherry Tesla Roadster with a spacesuited mannequin, Starman, as a mass simulator; about 1,250 kg with batteries (JPL Horizons) or 1,300 kg at launch (Wikipedia)
credit: Sources: SpaceX Falcon Heavy press kit (February 2018), Spaceflight Now's launch timeline, Wikipedia (Falcon Heavy test flight; Elon Musk's Tesla Roadster; Landing Zones 1 and 2), JPL Horizons (target -143205, "Tesla Roadster (AKA: Starman, 2018-017A)"), Space.com and NASA History. Every time after liftoff is the pre-launch plan from the press kit and Spaceflight Now; the actual times were not found, except the third burn's completion, which JPL Horizons gives as about 02:30 UTC on 7 February. There is no arrival: arrival_date and transit_days mark the car's closest passage to Mars, 7 October 2020. Source conflicts: the centre core hit the sea at about 500 km/h (Wikipedia, Musk) or 484 km/h (Space.com); Mars passage about 8 million km (Wikipedia) or 7.4 million km (JPL Horizons); aphelion 1.66 au (Wikipedia) or 1.674 au (Horizons elements, epoch 15 February 2018); the car's model year is 2008 (Wikipedia, test flight) or 2010 (Wikipedia, Roadster article).

launch.source: SpaceX Falcon Heavy press kit (February 2018): 27 Merlin engines, more than 5 million pounds of thrust. No C3 or injected mass is published in the sources used

events.label: Launch — Falcon Heavy's first flight
events.description: Launch Complex 39A, Kennedy Space Center, 6 February 2018 at 20:45 UTC, inside the planned 1:30-4:00 pm EST window (the exact second of liftoff is not in the sources used). 27 Merlin engines, more than 5 million pounds of thrust. Both side cores were flight-proven: one had flown Thaicom 8 (May 2016), the other CRS-9 (July 2016).

events.label: Side boosters land at LZ-1 and LZ-2
events.description: Planned: the side cores separate at 00:02:33 and land at 00:07:58 on Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral, one planned time for both; actual times not found. They touched down nearly simultaneously. Wikipedia's LZ page puts B1023 on LZ-1 and B1025 on LZ-2; no second source says which landed where.

events.label: Centre core lost at sea beside the drone ship
events.description: Planned landing on the drone ship Of Course I Still Love You at 00:08:19. Two of the three landing engines did not relight; Musk said there was not enough ignition fluid to light the outer two. The core hit the water about 100 m from the ship at about 500 km/h (Wikipedia, Musk) or 484 km/h (Space.com) and damaged two of the ship's thrusters.

events.label: Second burn, then the long coast
events.description: Planned: first cutoff of the second stage (SECO-1) at 00:08:31, restart at 00:28:22, second cutoff (SECO-2) at 00:28:52. The press kit then lists "an experimental long coast and third stage two burn": about six hours coasting through the Van Allen radiation belts (Wikipedia). Actual times not found.

events.label: Third burn: past Mars orbit
events.description: Planned at T+06:00:00; JPL Horizons says the burn was completed at about 02:30 UTC on 7 February, 5 h 45 min after liftoff. The plan was a precessing Earth-Mars elliptical orbit around the Sun. Musk: "Third burn successful. Exceeded Mars orbit and kept going to the Asteroid Belt." The Horizons elements give an aphelion of 1.674 au (Wikipedia: 1.66 au).

events.label: Closest passage to Mars
events.description: 7 October 2020. JPL Horizons predicts a closest approach of 0.0495 au (7.4 million km) at about 06:26 TDB; Wikipedia says about 8 million km. Wikipedia reports no significant effect on the car's orbit.
